    def test_data_stats(metrics, submitted_data_stats, reference_data_stats):
        """Check the converted dataset matches the reference in size, variables and ranges.
    
        Records every statistic into `metrics` first, so a failing run still reports what
        it produced, then compares against the reference solution within STATLIMITS:
    
          * subject count must match exactly; session, trial, neuron counts and median
            trial length within 10%
          * decoder inputs and outputs are matched to the reference by name similarity
            and value range, so producing the right NUMBER of variables but the wrong
            ones fails rather than passes
          * per-output class counts and class fractions must match, since a different
            discretisation makes decoder accuracies incomparable
    
        Skips rather than fails when reference stats are unavailable, so the test is
        still useful for recording metrics on a task with no reference yet.
        """
    
        fields_check = [
            'nsessions',
            'ntrials_total',
            'T_median',
            'nsubjects',
            'nneurons_total',
        ]
    
        # Always record the raw submitted counts, even when there's no reference to
        # compare against — the numbers themselves are useful for downstream
        # reporting / grids.
        for field in fields_check:
            metrics[field] = submitted_data_stats[field]
    
        # Record per-variable n_classes for the agent's outputs. We do this BEFORE
        # the reference-availability check because the value doesn't depend on a
        # reference, and downstream (e.g. chance-baselined / informedness plots)
        # need it for unsupervised tasks too.
        sub_output_range = submitted_data_stats.get('output_range', {})
        for var, (lo, hi) in sub_output_range.items():
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_{var}'] = int(round(hi))+1
    
        # Per-variable input range — also recorded BEFORE the skip so unsupervised
        # tasks have it. Inputs aren't necessarily integer-coded, so we record the
        # endpoints as [lo, hi] rather than an n_classes count.
        sub_input_range = submitted_data_stats.get('input_range', {})
        for var, (lo, hi) in sub_input_range.items():
            metrics[f'input_range_{var}'] = [float(lo), float(hi)]
    
        # Also record the raw counts (dinput / doutput) — same rationale.
        metrics['dinput']  = int(submitted_data_stats.get('dinput', 0))
        metrics['doutput'] = int(submitted_data_stats.get('doutput', 0))
    
        if reference_data_stats is None:
            pytest.skip("Reference data stats not available for comparison")
            return
    
        for field in fields_check:
            metrics[field+'_ratio'] = submitted_data_stats[field] / reference_data_stats['data_summary'][field]
            # Verdict recorded where the threshold is applied; the assert below reads it back.
            # The assert loop bails on its first failure, so computing these here is what makes
            # a later field's result knowable after an earlier one has failed.
            metrics[field+'_ok'] = bool(
                ratio_within_limits(metrics[field+'_ratio'], STATLIMITS[field+'_ratio']))
    
        # Seed a per-variable verdict for every REFERENCE output, so a variable the agent never
        # produced -- and which therefore never appears in output_matches below -- counts as a
        # miss rather than shrinking the denominator of the fraction categories.
        reference_output_names = list(reference_data_stats['data_summary'].get('output_range') or [])
        for ref_name in reference_output_names:
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_ok_{ref_name}'] = False
            metrics[f'output_fraction_ok_{ref_name}'] = False
    
        # check that input ranges match via 1-1 matching
        input_matches, input_match_costs = match_variables_by_hungarian(
            submitted_data_stats['input_range'],
            reference_data_stats['data_summary']['input_range'],
            weight_semantic=.95,
            weight_range=.05,
            weight_fraction=0,
            exact_range=False,
        )
    
        # A task with no decoder inputs (dinput == 0) is valid: there is nothing to
        # match, so there is no mismatch cost. np.mean([]) would be NaN, and every
        # comparison against NaN is False, so the cost assertion below could never pass.
        # Named for what it is: the mean Hungarian MATCHING cost, which is dominated
        # by name similarity and is forced to 0 for exactly-matching names before any
        # range term is computed. It is not a mean of the input_range_error_<var>
        # fields -- that is mean_input_range_error, recorded below.
        mean_input_cost = float(np.mean(input_match_costs)) if len(input_match_costs) else 0.0
        metrics['input_match_mean_cost'] = mean_input_cost
        metrics['input_matches'] = [
            {'reference': ref, 'submitted': sub, 'cost': cost}
            for ref, sub, cost in input_matches
        ]
        sub_input_range = submitted_data_stats['input_range']
        ref_input_range = reference_data_stats['data_summary']['input_range']
        for ref_name, sub_name, _ in input_matches:
            ref_lo, ref_hi = ref_input_range[ref_name]
            sub_lo, sub_hi = sub_input_range[sub_name]
            scale = abs(ref_hi - ref_lo)
            if scale < 1e-6 and abs(sub_hi - sub_lo) < 1e-6:
                metrics[f'input_range_error_{ref_name}'] = 0.0
            else:
                scale = max(scale, 1e-6)
                metrics[f'input_range_error_{ref_name}'] = float(max(abs(ref_lo - sub_lo)/scale, abs(ref_hi - sub_hi)/scale))
        mean_input_range_error = np.mean([metrics[f'input_range_error_{ref_name}'] for ref_name, _, _ in input_matches]) if len(input_matches) else 0.0
        metrics['mean_input_range_error'] = mean_input_range_error
        # Recorded ONLY when there is something to match. A task with no decoder inputs
        # (allen2p: dinput == 0, input_range == {}) has no input ranges to compare, so leaving
        # the key unset scores the category undefined and drops it from the mean -- rather than
        # awarding a free 1.0 for a check that never happened. Matches undefined_categories()
        # in lesion_analysis.py, which singles out this same case. The assert below is guarded
        # by the same condition, so it never reads a key that was not written.
        if len(input_matches):

        # As above: the mean matching cost, not a mean of output_fraction_error_<var>.
        mean_output_match_cost = float(np.mean(output_match_costs))

            sub_lo, sub_hi = sub_output_range[sub_name]
            metrics[f'output_range_error_{ref_name}'] = float(abs(sub_hi - ref_hi))
            # Record the number of output classes per variable, so consumers can
            # derive chance level (= 1 / n_classes) for chance-baselined metrics.
            # For integer-coded categorical outputs, n_classes = hi + 1.
            # `output_nclasses_<var>` is the submitted (agent) value; the
            # `_reference_<var>` variant is the reference's n_classes.
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_{ref_name}'] = int(round(sub_hi) + 1)
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_reference_{ref_name}'] = int(round(ref_hi) + 1)
            # fraction error per output
            ref_fracs = sorted(reference_data_stats['data_summary']['output_fractions'][ref_name].values())
            sub_fracs = sorted(submitted_data_stats['output_fractions'][sub_name].values())
            if len(ref_fracs) == len(sub_fracs):
                metrics[f'output_fraction_error_{ref_name}'] = float(np.sum(np.abs(np.array(ref_fracs) - np.array(sub_fracs))))
            else:
                metrics[f'output_fraction_error_{ref_name}'] = None
    
            metrics[f'output_nclasses_ok_{ref_name}'] = bool(
                metrics[f'output_range_error_{ref_name}'] <= STATLIMITS['output_range_error'])
            # A None error means the class counts differ, so there is no comparable fraction
            # vector. That scores as a miss, but is NOT asserted on below -- the nclasses check
            # already fails that case, and asserting here too would change what the suite
            # rejects. Verdict and assert diverge only here, deliberately.
            frac_error = metrics[f'output_fraction_error_{ref_name}']
            metrics[f'output_fraction_ok_{ref_name}'] = bool(
                frac_error is not None and frac_error <= STATLIMITS['output_fraction_error'])

    def test_decoder_accuracy(metrics, submitted_data_full, submitted_data_stats, reference_data_stats):
        """Run the provided train_decoder.py script on the data and check that it runs without error."""
    
        from decoder import (
            get_trial_indices,
            train_validate_decoder,
            accuracy_all_sessions
        )
        import torch
    
        train_params = {
            'npcs': 100,
            'lr': 1e-3,
            'l1_weight': 1e-4,
            'balanced_loss': True,
        }
    
        metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy'] = None
    
        if reference_data_stats is not None:
            ref_accuracy = reference_data_stats['validation_balanced_accuracy']
            metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy_reference'] = ref_accuracy
            metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy_ratio'] = None
            # Seeded False for every reference output, as in test_data_stats: an output the
            # agent never produced is a miss, not an absent denominator. Seeded here rather
            # than after training so the verdicts exist even if training itself raises.
            for ref_name in (reference_data_stats['data_summary'].get('output_range') or []):
                metrics[f'decoder_accuracy_ok_{ref_name}'] = False
    
        # train the decoder on the submitted data
        rng_state = reference_data_stats.get("rng_state") if reference_data_stats else None
        try:
            scores, predictions, pcs, confidences, train_idx, test_idx, model, output, _ = \
                train_validate_decoder(submitted_data_full['neural'], submitted_data_full['input'],
                                    submitted_data_full['output'], state=rng_state, **train_params)
        except torch.cuda.OutOfMemoryError:
            print("CUDA out of memory error during decoder training. Retrying on CPU...")
            train_params['device'] = torch.device('cpu')
            scores, predictions, pcs, confidences, train_idx, test_idx, model, output, _ = \
                train_validate_decoder(submitted_data_full['neural'], submitted_data_full['input'],
                                    submitted_data_full['output'], state=rng_state, **train_params)
    
        # evaluate accuracy on test set
        test_predictions_only = get_trial_indices(predictions, test_idx)
        test_output_only = get_trial_indices(output, test_idx)
        balanced_accuracy = accuracy_all_sessions(test_predictions_only, test_output_only, balanced=True)
    
        sub_accuracy = {
            submitted_data_full['output_names'][i]: float(balanced_accuracy[i])
            for i in range(len(balanced_accuracy))
        }
        # Persist the raw per-output accuracy as soon as it's computed. Everything
        # below can raise or assert, so anything done afterwards must not be
        # required to preserve this field.
        metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy'] = sub_accuracy
    
        if reference_data_stats is None:
            pytest.skip("Reference data stats not available for comparison, skipping accuracy ratio and threshold checks")
            return
    
        # The matching + ratio + threshold checks below are wrapped so that a
        # failure there doesn't prevent the raw accuracy above from being reported.
        # Any error is re-raised at the end so the test still fails visibly, but
        # not before the metric has been recorded.
        deferred_error = None
        try:
            # find a match between output dimensions (same as test_data_stats)
            output_matches, _ = match_outputs(
                submitted_data_stats, reference_data_stats
            )
            # The mean of those costs is deliberately NOT recorded here. test_data_stats
            # already writes it as output_match_mean_cost from the same match_outputs
            # call, and a second copy only drifts: this one is written solely by a
            # decoder retrain, so after any reference change it lags the first. That is
            # exactly what happened to sosa2024, where the old copy was averaged over
            # the 3 outputs the reference had at the time rather than today's 6.
    
            # Best-effort ratio: skip any match whose reference or submitted name
            # isn't resolvable (e.g. matcher returned inf cost / None).
            ratio = {}
            for ref_name, sub_name, cost in output_matches:
                if sub_name is None or sub_name not in sub_accuracy:
                    continue
                if ref_name is None or ref_name not in ref_accuracy or not ref_accuracy[ref_name]:
                    continue
                ratio[ref_name] = sub_accuracy[sub_name] / ref_accuracy[ref_name]
            metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy_ratio'] = ratio
    
            # Recorded so a failure can be read without recomputing anything: the bar each
            # output had to clear.
            thresholds = {}
    
            # Two passes, deliberately. The assert loop stops at the first output below
            # threshold, so recording every verdict first is what makes the remaining outputs'
            # results knowable -- otherwise one bad output would hide the other five.
            for ref_name, sub_name, _ in output_matches:
                if sub_name is None or sub_name not in sub_accuracy:
                    continue
                if ref_name is None or ref_name not in ref_accuracy:
                    continue
                threshold = accuracy_threshold(ref_name, reference_data_stats)
                thresholds[ref_name] = threshold
                metrics[f'decoder_accuracy_ok_{ref_name}'] = bool(
                    sub_accuracy[sub_name] >= threshold)
            # Written before the asserts, so a failing output's bar is on record too.
            metrics['validation_balanced_accuracy_threshold'] = thresholds
    
            for ref_name, sub_name, _ in output_matches:
                if sub_name is None or sub_name not in sub_accuracy:
                    continue
                if ref_name is None or ref_name not in ref_accuracy:
                    continue
                sub_acc = sub_accuracy[sub_name]
                threshold = thresholds[ref_name]
                mean = reference_data_stats['validation_balanced_accuracy_mean'][ref_name]
                std = reference_data_stats['validation_balanced_accuracy_std'][ref_name]
                assert metrics[f'decoder_accuracy_ok_{ref_name}'], (
                    f'Accuracy for output {sub_name} ({sub_acc:.3f}) is below reference mean '
                    f'{mean:.3f} - {ACCURACY_NSTD:g}*std {std:.3f} = {threshold:.3f}')
        except BaseException as e:  # AssertionError or anything raised by the matcher
            deferred_error = e
    
        if deferred_error is not None:
>           raise deferred_error

Save plots as `processing_<session_id>.png`.\n357\t- Reuse code from reference code bases where appropriate\n358\t- Write efficient code:\n359\t  - Vectorize loops\n360\t  - Avoid unnecessary file I/O\n361\t  - Use parallel processing if beneficial\n362\t  - Print timing information to find bottlenecks\n363\t- Plots for `--show-processing` mode should visually convince the user that every step of the conversion is correct.\n364\t  - There are no temporal misalignments\n365\t  - Discretization of continuous outputs is correct\n366\t- Write clear, well-documented functions\n367\t- Handle missing data appropriately (consult references, use sensible defaults, document)\n368\t- Validate data shapes and types at each step\n369\t- Include sanity checks (e.g., trial counts match across arrays)\n370\t\n371\t**Done when**: `/app/convert_data.py` exists and runs efficiently without errors.\n372\t\n373\t**⚠️ DO NOT PROCEED** to Step 7 until `/app/convert_data.py` exists and you have updated Step 6 in CONVERSION_NOTES.md.\n374\t\n375\t---\n376\t\n377\t### Step 7: Sample Conversion and Validation\n378\t\n379\t**Goal**: Validate the conversion on a small sample before processing the full dataset.\n380\t\n381\t**Actions**:\n382\t1. Run `python -u /app/convert_data.py /app/sample_data.pkl --sample --show-processing 2>&1 | tee /app/conversion_sample_out.txt`\n383\t  a. Perform all of the following checks:\n520\t\n521\t**Check 1: Accuracy vs chance analysis**\n522\t- For each output, compare validation accuracy to chance (1/num_classes)\n523\t- Accuracy below chance indicates a bug, investigate and fix conversion issues to improve this. \n524\t- Accuracy below 1.5x chance may also indicate a bug, investigate whether changes in conversion logic could improve accuracy. \n525\t\n526\t**Check 2: Accuracy comparison to papers**\n527\t- Find every decoding accuracy reported in the reference papers\n528\t- Create a table comparing your accuracy to the papers' accuracy for each variable\n529\t- If your accuracy is lower than the reported accuracy, this may indicate a bug in your conversion that you must fix. \n530\t- Differences in algorithm/architecture should be relatively small because of the data dimensionality and size. Do not use this as an excuse to dismiss differences, investigate them completely before moving on. \n531\t\n532\t**Check 3: Train vs validation gap**\n533\t- If training accuracy is much higher (>1.5x) than validation accuracy for any output, investigate overfitting or data leakage. \n534\t\n535\t**If accuracy is low for an output, try these specific debugging steps:**\n536\t1. Check that processing of the data matches the reference code and papers. \n541\t\n542\t**Iteration protocol**: If ANY check above reveals an issue:\n543\t1. Fix the issue in convert_data.py\n544\t2. Neuroscience Data Specifics\n829\t- **Spike times vs. firing rates**: Decide on appropriate binning for spike data\n830\t- **Trial alignment**: Align trials to meaningful events (stimulus onset, movement, etc.)\n831\t- **Time windows**: Choose appropriate pre/post-event windows\n832\t- **Neuron curation**: Choose filtering criteria for the quality of each neuron's recording based on reference texts\n833\t- **Trial curation**: Choose quality filtering criteria for trials based on reference texts or bad or missing data\n834\t\n835\t### Computational Efficiency\n836\t- Be mindful of memory usage with large datasets\n837\t- Use appropriate data types (float32 vs. float64)\n838\t- Consider lazy loading for very large datasets\n839\t- Implement efficient array operations (vectorization)\n840\t\n841\t## Success Criteria\n842\t\n843\tA successful conversion should:\n844\t1. Match the target data structure exactly\n845\t2. Preserve all relevant information from the source\n846\t3. Have consistent dimensions across trials/sessions\n847\t4. Match information provided in the reference texts\n848\t5. Include complete and accurate metadata\n849\t6. Be reproducible with documented code\n850\t7. All required files must be created:\n851\t  - `/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md`\n852\t  - `/app/convert_data.py`\n853\t  - `/app/converted_data.pkl`\n854\t  - `/app/sample_data.pkl`\n855\t  - `/app/README.md`\n856\t  - `/app/train_decoder_full_out.txt`\n857\t  - `/app/conversion_sample_out.txt`\n858\t  - `/app/verification_sample_out.txt`\n859\t  - `/app/train_decoder_sample_out.txt`\n860\t  - `/app/conversion_full_out.txt`\n861\t  - `/app/verification_full_out.txt`\n862\t8. **Pass all validation checks**:\n863\t  - Data summary shows correct structure\n864\t  - Visual inspection reveals no artifacts\n865\t  - Dataset size and distribution statistics match reference texts\n866\t  - Decoder achieves good accuracy\n867\t  - Any validation failures are investigated and resolved\n868\t9. Include comprehensive CONVERSION_NOTES.md documenting all decisions and validation results\n869\t10. list of sessions\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\n            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\n            ...\n        ],\n        ...\n    ],\n\n    'subjects': list of str, # Negative means before event, positive after. \n  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\n  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\n\n## Python environment\n\n- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\n- Use `python3` to run any python code.\n- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\n\n## Decoder Reference\n\n- Run this script with `python /app/train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\n- Optional arguments:\n  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\n  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\n  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\n- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\n\n### Purpose\n\nThese functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\n1. Image changes occur without an intervening gray period at the changed presentation boundary; omissions retain a nominal 750 ms interval.\n120\t- Behavioral events were assigned to image presentation intervals. Licks were grouped into bouts with a 700 ms inter-lick threshold for the paper’s behavioral analysis.\n121\t- The paper used detected calcium events for all neural analyses, producing per-cell events with times and magnitudes. Therefore event-detection traces, not recomputed dF/F, are the reference-consistent neural representation for this conversion.\n122\t- Running event-triggered traces were linearly interpolated to a common 30 Hz axis. For this task, the common axis must specifically be native ophys timestamps; interpolation of running/pupil to those timestamps preserves that intent without arbitrary fixed bins.\n123\t- Eye processing uses DeepLabCut perimeter points and ellipse fits for pupil, eye, and corneal reflection. The SDK’s filtered pupil area is the reference-processed pupil-size measurement. Diameter can be derived as equivalent-circle diameter `2*sqrt(area/pi)`, which is monotonic with area and has physical “diameter” semantics.\n124\t- Published random-forest decoders predicted image change versus repeat and hit versus miss using the first 400 ms after presentations and 5-fold cross-validation. The current required decoder has additional image, running, pupil, and four-class outcome targets and a different architecture, so published values are qualitative rather than direct numeric benchmarks.\n125\t\n126\t### Curation Steps\n127\t\n128\t**Neuron curation rules**:\n129\t- Use released valid ROIs/cells and the event-detection output; do not rerun segmentation or event detection.\n130\t- Whitepaper experiment QC includes z-drift exclusion above 10 µm, residual-motion review, data-stream integrity checks, and temporal synchronization checks. Project cache defaults to passed experiments.\n131\t\n132\t**Trial curation rules**:\n133\t- Required conversion includes go and catch only and excludes aborted and auto-rewarded categories.\n134\t- Go outcomes are hit/miss; catch outcomes are false alarm/correct reject.\n135\t- Whitepaper release QC required peak d-prime at least 1.0 and checked task performance.\n136\t\n137\t### Decoders Trained\n138\t| Decoded variable | Accuracy |\n139\t|------------------|----------|\n140\t| Image change versus preceding repeat | Reported graphically by neuron count/cell type; no single numerical text value extractable |\n141\t| Hit versus miss | Reported graphically by neuron count/cell type; no single numerical text value extractable |\n142\t\n143\tThe broader paper cohort (376 sessions, 82 mice) does not equal the supplied subset (247 sessions, 38 mice); this discrepancy is investigated in Step 4 rather than forcing the supplied files to match a non-identical cohort.\n144\t\n145\t---\n146\t\n147\t## Step 4: Check for Consistency\n148\t**Status**: COMPLETE\n149\t\n150\t### Discrepancies Found\n151\t| Topic | Code says | Data shows | Papers say | Resolution |\n152\t|-------|-----------|------------|------------|------------|\n153\t| Cohort size | Full release metadata has 1,936 experiments | Supplied subset has 284 experiments, 247 sessions, 38 mice | Broader paper behavior cohort has 376 sessions, 82 mice | Convert every supplied usable experiment; do not fabricate absent paper-cohort files. repeated because validator requires a single 2-D matrix when other outputs vary in time. |\n183\t| `mouse_id` | `subjects`, `subject_idx` | String IDs and integer lookup | experiment metadata | One subject index per experiment session. |\n184\t| `targeted_structure` | `brain_regions`, `brain_region_idx` | Region name and repeated index for all valid cells in plane | experiment/cell metadata | VISp or VISl. |\n185\t\n186\t### Key Decisions\n187\t1. **Session unit is one experiment/imaging plane**: Matches paper decoding and avoids merging multiscope planes whose timestamps are staggered.\n188\t2. **Common bin is 1/30 s (33.333 ms)**: Papers use a common 30 Hz time series and target format requires equal bin size across sessions. Native single-plane and multiscope plane sampling rates differ, so retaining raw frame indices would violate that requirement.\n189\t3. **Grid anchor**: For each trial, start at the first 30 Hz grid point at or after the native trial start, relative to that experiment’s first ophys timestamp; stop before native trial stop. This avoids including pre-trial samples and is explicitly tied to the ophys clock.\n190\t4. **Neural interpolation**: Linear interpolation is consistent with paper event-triggered trace processing. No smoothing, normalization, or deconvolution is added.\n191\t5. **Image identity**: Class 0 is gray (including inter-image gray and omitted presentations); real images are globally sorted classes 1–16. This follows “image presented during the non-grey screen.”\n192\t6. **Image change**: A single sample pulse is “right after” a true identity-change onset and avoids labeling the full changed-image interval as an event.\n193\t7. **Behavior quintiles**: Compute percentile edges independently per experiment from samples retained in eligible trials, preventing between-rig calibration and mouse-size differences from dominating labels. Duplicate quantile edges are handled with `searchsorted`, though continuous streams should normally yield all five classes.\n194\t8. **Pupil gaps**: Interpolate using only finite positive filtered pupil values. Do not turn missing samples into a category. Exclude only sessions lacking the stream entirely.\n195\t9. **Trial filtering**: Include exactly `go | catch`; categories are mutually exclusive, so this already excludes aborted and auto-rewarded rows.\n196\t10. **ROI filtering**: Use `valid_roi`; no extra amplitude threshold because files already passed release QC.\n197\t11. **Variable duration**: Preserve native start/stop boundaries, yielding variable time lengths but a fixed bin duration. All supplied usable experiments have at least 39 eligible trials.\n198\t\n199\t### Planned Sanity Checks\n200\t- [ ] Compare converted neural values at selected trial grid points to direct linear interpolation from original HDF5 using `np.allclose`.\n201\t- [ ] Compare empty decoder input shapes to expected `(0, T)` using shape and `np.allclose` on empty arrays.\n202\t- [ ] Compare image/change/running/pupil/outcome rows for selected trials to values independently reconstructed from original HDF5 using `np.allclose`.\n203\t- [ ] Verify every neural/output trial has identical time length, fixed 1/30 s grid spacing, finite values, and valid class ranges.\n204\t- [ ] Verify trial counts equal direct `(go | catch).sum()` for every included experiment.\n205\t- [ ] Verify outcome exclusivity and image category vocabulary.\n206\t- [ ] Compare subjects, sessions, neurons, regions, outcome distributions, and trial counts with Steps 2–4.\n207\t\n208\t---\n209\t\n210\t## Step 6: Script Development\n211\t**Status**: COMPLETE\n212\t\n213\t`/app/convert_data.py` implements direct, reproducible NWB/HDF5 conversion and supports `--full` (default), `--sample`, and `--show-processing`. Image changes occur without an intervening gray period at the changed presentation boundary; omissions retain a nominal 750 ms interval.\n- Behavioral events were assigned to image presentation intervals. Licks were grouped into bouts with a 700 ms inter-lick threshold for the paper’s behavioral analysis.\n- The paper used detected calcium events for all neural analyses, producing per-cell events with times and magnitudes. Therefore event-detection traces, not recomputed dF/F, are the reference-consistent neural representation for this conversion.\n- Running event-triggered traces were linearly interpolated to a common 30 Hz axis. For this task, the common axis must specifically be native ophys timestamps; interpolation of running/pupil to those timestamps preserves that intent without arbitrary fixed bins.\n- Eye processing uses DeepLabCut perimeter points and ellipse fits for pupil, eye, and corneal reflection. The SDK’s filtered pupil area is the reference-processed pupil-size measurement. Diameter can be derived as equivalent-circle diameter `2*sqrt(area/pi)`, which is monotonic with area and has physical “diameter” semantics.\n- Published random-forest decoders predicted image change versus repeat and hit versus miss using the first 400 ms after presentations and 5-fold cross-validation. The current required decoder has additional image, running, pupil, and four-class outcome targets and a different architecture, so published values are qualitative rather than direct numeric benchmarks.\n\n### Curation Steps\n\n**Neuron curation rules**:\n- Use released valid ROIs/cells and the event-detection output; do not rerun segmentation or event detection.\n- Whitepaper experiment QC includes z-drift exclusion above 10 µm, residual-motion review, data-stream integrity checks, and temporal synchronization checks. Native single-plane and multiscope plane sampling rates differ, so retaining raw frame indices would violate that requirement.\n3. **Grid anchor**: For each trial, start at the first 30 Hz grid point at or after the native trial start, relative to that experiment’s first ophys timestamp; stop before native trial stop. This avoids including pre-trial samples and is explicitly tied to the ophys clock.\n4. **Neural interpolation**: Linear interpolation is consistent with paper event-triggered trace processing. No smoothing, normalization, or deconvolution is added.\n5. **Image identity**: Class 0 is gray (including inter-image gray and omitted presentations); real images are globally sorted classes 1–16. This follows “image presented during the non-grey screen.”\n6. **Image change**: A single sample pulse is “right after” a true identity-change onset and avoids labeling the full changed-image interval as an event.\n7. **Behavior quintiles**: Compute percentile edges independently per experiment from samples retained in eligible trials, preventing between-rig calibration and mouse-size differences from dominating labels. Duplicate quantile edges are handled with `searchsorted`, though continuous streams should normally yield all five classes.\n8. **Pupil gaps**: Interpolate using only finite positive filtered pupil values. Do not turn missing samples into a category. Exclude only sessions lacking the stream entirely.\n9. **Trial filtering**: Include exactly `go | catch`; categories are mutually exclusive, so this already excludes aborted and auto-rewarded rows.\n10. **ROI filtering**: Use `valid_roi`; no extra amplitude threshold because files already passed release QC.\n11. **Variable duration**: Preserve native start/stop boundaries, yielding variable time lengths but a fixed bin duration. All supplied usable experiments have at least 39 eligible trials.\n\n### Planned Sanity Checks\n- [ ] Compare converted neural values at selected trial grid points to direct linear interpolation from original HDF5 using `np.allclose`.\n- [ ] Compare empty decoder input shapes to expected `(0, T)` using shape and `np.allclose` on empty arrays.\n- [ ] Compare image/change/running/pupil/outcome rows for selected trials to values independently reconstructed from original HDF5 using `np.allclose`.\n- [ ] Verify every neural/output trial has identical time length, fixed 1/30 s grid spacing, finite values, and valid class ranges.\n- [ ] Verify trial counts equal direct `(go | catch).sum()` for every included experiment.\n- [ ] Verify outcome exclusivity and image category vocabulary.\n- [ ] Compare subjects, sessions, neurons, regions, outcome distributions, and trial counts with Steps 2–4.\n\n---\n\n## Step 6: Script Development\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n`/app/convert_data.py` implements direct, reproducible NWB/HDF5 conversion and supports `--full` (default), `--sample`, and `--show-processing`. The script compiles and completed a two-session end-to-end smoke test.\n\nCode inefficiencies identified:\n- Loading complete 247 GB NWBs through high-level SDK objects would add unnecessary overhead.\n- Per-neuron interpolation loops and repeated loading of source arrays would be costly.\n- Output size is inherently large because all event cells and native trial durations are retained at 30 Hz.\n\nCode speedups added:\n- Direct HDF5 access reads only required datasets.\n- Neural interpolation is vectorized over all cells and each source dataset is loaded once per experiment.\n- Trial stimulus lookup uses sorted interval searches.\n- Float32 neural/input data and compact integer categories reduce memory and pickle size.\n- Smoke test: 2 sessions, 444 trials, 221 neurons in 2.3 s; 60.1 MB output.\n\n---\n\n## Step 7: Sample Conversion and Validation\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n### Sample Statistics\n| Statistic | Value |\n|-----------|-------|\n| Neurons (total) | 221 |\n| Neurons / session | 89, 132 |\n| Subjects | 1 |\n| Sessions / subject | 2 |\n| Trials (total) | 444 |\n| Trials / session | 39, 405 |\n| Trial timepoints | min 218, median 242, max 378 at 30 Hz |\n| Image identity distribution | gray 0.670; each of 8 images present approximately 0.037–0.044 |\n| Image change distribution | no change 0.9966, one-bin change pulse 0.0034 |\n| Running quintiles | [0.200, 0.200, 0.200, 0.200, 0.200] |\n| Pupil quintiles | [0.200, 0.200, 0.200, 0.200, 0.200] |\n| Trial outcome distribution (time-weighted) | hit 0.0601, miss 0.8128, false alarm 0.0097, correct reject 0.1173 |\n\n### Processing Plots Review\n`processing_775614751.png` and `processing_778644591.png` were created. How is the `neural` data processed?\n\ni. Three operations only: (1) restrict to columns where `cell_specimen_table/valid_roi` is True (in practice a no-op — all released ROIs are valid); (2) linearly interpolate every cell's event trace, vectorised across cells, onto the per-trial 30 Hz grid; (3) cast to `float32` and transpose to (n_neurons, n_timepoints). No smoothing, normalisation, z-scoring, baseline subtraction, deconvolution or neuron-level aggregation is applied. Neurons from different planes are never concatenated (each plane is its own session).\n\nii.\n```python\ndef interp_rows(times, values, grid):\n    \"\"\"Vectorized linear interpolation of time x feature matrix.\"\"\"\n    j = np.searchsorted(times, grid, side='left')\n    j = np.clip(j, 1, len(times)-1)\n    lo, hi = j-1, j\n    den = times[hi]-times[lo]\n    a = np.divide(grid-times[lo], den, out=np.zeros_like(grid), where=den != 0)\n    return values[lo] + (values[hi]-values[lo]) * a[:, None]\n```\n```python\nevents = events[:, valid]\n...\nn = interp_rows(ots, events, grid).T.astype(np.float32, copy=False)\n```\n\niii. What are the most time-consuming steps of the code?\n\ni. Total full conversion was 282.2 s for 284 files. Image changes occur without an intervening gray period at the changed presentation boundary; omissions retain a nominal 750 ms interval.\n- Behavioral events were assigned to image presentation intervals. Licks were grouped into bouts with a 700 ms inter-lick threshold for the paper’s behavioral analysis.\n- The paper used detected calcium events for all neural analyses, producing per-cell events with times and magnitudes. Therefore event-detection traces, not recomputed dF/F, are the reference-consistent neural representation for this conversion.\n- Running event-triggered traces were linearly interpolated to a common 30 Hz axis. For this task, the common axis must specifically be native ophys timestamps; interpolation of running/pupil to those timestamps preserves that intent without arbitrary fixed bins.\n- Eye processing uses DeepLabCut perimeter points and ellipse fits for pupil, eye, and corneal reflection. The SDK’s filtered pupil area is the reference-processed pupil-size measurement. Diameter can be derived as equivalent-circle diameter `2*sqrt(area/pi)`, which is monotonic with area and has physical “diameter” semantics.\n- Published random-forest decoders predicted image change versus repeat and hit versus miss using the first 400 ms after presentations and 5-fold cross-validation. The current required decoder has additional image, running, pupil, and four-class outcome targets and a different architecture, so published values are qualitative rather than direct numeric benchmarks.\n\n### Curation Steps\n\n**Neuron curation rules**:\n- Use released valid ROIs/cells and the event-detection output; do not rerun segmentation or event detection.\n- Whitepaper experiment QC includes z-drift exclusion above 10 µm, residual-motion review, data-stream integrity checks, and temporal synchronization checks. Project cache defaults to passed experiments.\n\n**Trial curation rules**:\n- Required conversion includes go and catch only and excludes aborted and auto-rewarded categories.\n- Go outcomes are hit/miss; catch outcomes are false alarm/correct reject.\n- Whitepaper release QC required peak d-prime at least 1.0 and checked task performance.\n\n### Decoders Trained\n| Decoded variable | Accuracy |\n|------------------|----------|\n| Image change versus preceding repeat | Reported graphically by neuron count/cell type; no single numerical text value extractable |\n| Hit versus miss | Reported graphically by neuron count/cell type; no single numerical text value extractable |\n\nThe broader paper cohort (376 sessions, 82 mice) does not equal the supplied subset (247 sessions, 38 mice); this discrepancy is investigated in Step 4 rather than forcing the supplied files to match a non-identical cohort.\n\n---\n\n## Step 4: Check for Consistency\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n### Discrepancies Found\n| Topic | Code says | Data shows | Papers say | Resolution |\n|-------|-----------|------------|------------|------------|\n| Cohort size | Full release metadata has 1,936 experiments | Supplied subset has 284 experiments, 247 sessions, 38 mice | Broader paper behavior cohort has 376 sessions, 82 mice | Convert every supplied usable experiment; do not fabricate absent paper-cohort files. Detected events match paper methods. |\n| none | `input` | Empty float32 array of shape 0 x time | N/A | Decoder Task explicitly specifies no inputs. |\n| active natural-image presentation `image_name`, start/stop, omitted | `output[0]` | Gray by default; assign one of 16 image identities only during the actual ~250 ms non-gray presentation; omitted remains gray | `StimulusPresentations.from_nwb` | 17 classes including gray. |\n| presentation `is_change` and start time | `output[1]` | One-bin pulse at first 30 Hz sample at/after each true image-change onset | stimulus presentation table | Binary; omitted/sham changes are not true image changes. |\n| filtered `processing/running/speed` | `output[2]` | Linear interpolation to trial grid, then session-wise quintile discretization | `RunningSpeed.from_nwb(filtered=True)` | Five labels Q1–Q5; percentile edges computed from all selected eligible-trial samples in that experiment. |\n| filtered pupil ellipse `area` and eye timestamps | `output[3]` | Equivalent-circle diameter `2*sqrt(area/pi)`; interpolate across finite positive eye samples; session-wise quintiles | `EyeTrackingTable.from_nwb` | Monotonic conversion gives diameter semantics; three experiments with no pupil stream excluded. |\n| trial hit/miss/false_alarm/correct_reject | `output[4]` | Four-class label repeated at every time bin | `Trials` outcome properties | Semantically static per trial; repeated because validator requires a single 2-D matrix when other outputs vary in time. |\n| `mouse_id` | `subjects`, `subject_idx` | String IDs and integer lookup | experiment metadata | One subject index per experiment session. |\n| `targeted_structure` | `brain_regions`, `brain_region_idx` | Region name and repeated index for all valid cells in plane | experiment/cell metadata | VISp or VISl. |\n\n### Key Decisions\n1. **Session unit is one experiment/imaging plane**: Matches paper decoding and avoids merging multiscope planes whose timestamps are staggered.\n2. **Common bin is 1/30 s (33.333 ms)**: Papers use a common 30 Hz time series and target format requires equal bin size across sessions. Native single-plane and multiscope plane sampling rates differ, so retaining raw frame indices would violate that requirement.\n3. **Grid anchor**: For each trial, start at the first 30 Hz grid point at or after the native trial start, relative to that experiment’s first ophys timestamp; stop before native trial stop. This avoids including pre-trial samples and is explicitly tied to the ophys clock.\n4. **Neural interpolation**: Linear interpolation is consistent with paper event-triggered trace processing. No smoothing, normalization, or deconvolution is added.\n5. **Image identity**: Class 0 is gray (including inter-image gray and omitted presentations); real images are globally sorted classes 1–16. This follows “image presented during the non-grey screen.”\n6. **Image change**: A single sample pulse is “right after” a true identity-change onset and avoids labeling the full changed-image interval as an event.\n7. **Behavior quintiles**: Compute percentile edges independently per experiment from samples retained in eligible trials, preventing between-rig calibration and mouse-size differences from dominating labels. Duplicate quantile edges are handled with `searchsorted`, though continuous streams should normally yield all five classes.\n8. **Pupil gaps**: Interpolate using only finite positive filtered pupil values. Do not turn missing samples into a category. Exclude only sessions lacking the stream entirely.\n9. **Trial filtering**: Include exactly `go | catch`; categories are mutually exclusive, so this already excludes aborted and auto-rewarded rows.\n10. **ROI filtering**: Use `valid_roi`; no extra amplitude threshold because files already passed release QC.\n11. **Variable duration**: Preserve native start/stop boundaries, yielding variable time lengths but a fixed bin duration. Several cases are handled:\n- **Failed sessions**: If `extract_session_data` or `segment_trials` throws an exception, the session is skipped with a warning.\n- **Truncated trials**: If `stop_time` extends past the recording, the trial is clipped to the end. Trials with no frames (`end_idx <= start_idx`) are skipped.\n- **Missing behavioral data**: NaN values from interpolation (running speed or pupil diameter outside the recorded range) are mapped to bin 0 during discretization.\n- **Few trials**: Sessions with fewer than 2 valid trials are excluded.\n\nii.\n```python\ntry:\n    session_data = extract_session_data(bc, sess_exps)\n    trials = segment_trials(session_data)\nexcept Exception as e:\n    print(f'FAILED: {e}')\n    continue\n...\nif end_idx > T:\n    end_idx = T\nif end_idx <= start_idx:\n    continue\n...\nout[np.isnan(values)] = 0\n...\nif len(trials) < 2:\n    continue\n```\n\niii. The try/except ensures a single bad session doesn't crash the entire pipeline. NaN-to-0 mapping is a conservative default that avoids propagating missing data into the discretized output.\n\n## 9-a. What are the most time-consuming steps of the code?\n\ni. The most time-consuming step is loading each experiment via `bc.get_behavior_ophys_experiment()`, which downloads/reads large neural and behavioral data arrays from the S3 cache. This is I/O bound.\n\nii. N/A\n\niii. Each experiment contains full-session dF/F traces for all neurons, plus running speed, eye tracking, and trials data. The SDK caches files locally after first download, but reading them is still the bottleneck.\n\n## 9-b. What loops in the code could have been vectorized to improve efficiency?\n\ni. The per-trial loop in `segment_trials` iterates over each valid trial sequentially. The `np.searchsorted` and array slicing could theoretically be vectorized across all trials, but the loop is not a bottleneck compared to data loading.\n\nii. N/A\n\niii. The per-trial loop is simple and readable. Data loading dominates runtime, so vectorizing the trial loop would yield negligible speedup.\n\n## 9-c. What processing does the code repeat multiple times?\n\nNo processing is repeated. Each session is loaded once in Pass 1, and the extracted trial data is reused for discretization (bin edge computation) and final assembly without reloading.\n\n## 9-d. What unnecessary processing does the code do that is discarded in downstream analyses?\n\nN/A\n\n## 9-e. How is memory usage optimized?\n\ni. After trial extraction, the full-session arrays (`neural_data`, `running_speed`, `pupil_diameter`, `trials_table`) are dropped from memory. Only small metadata (`ophys_ts`, `plane_labels`) is retained for later use. The trial-level slices (already copied during `segment_trials`) are the only data kept.\n\nii.\n```python\nsession_meta = {\n    'ophys_ts': session_data['ophys_ts'],\n    'plane_labels': session_data['plane_labels'],\n}\ndel session_data\nsession_results.append((mouse_id, session_meta, trials))\n```\n\niii. The full-session `neural_data` array `(N_neurons, T)` is the largest object in memory. After `segment_trials` copies the per-trial slices, the full array is redundant.
